  1. Mostly those directly affected by those rules even bother to care

  2. Even among those directly affected, they are unlikely to leave.

  3. There is nowhere good to go, thanks to the large and diverse community that reinforces itself.

  4. Breaking up of communities separates people and creates long periods of separation. In the case of Napster, the community is still scattered today. It never recovered.

You answered the question in your reply by stating the problem.

Allowing any large central figure to control what speech is or is not considered acceptable will always be a problem. That includes anything from the government to large sites like Reddit and Twitter.

In the beginning the web was incredibly decentralized but Web 2.0 trends saw sites like Facebook (Replacing personally run blogs), Twitter (Replacing IRC) , and Reddit (Replacing Usenet) take hold.

Why did this happen? Most of those sites are user friendly, attractive, easy to use, they have large communities, and most importantly they're free*.

TL;DR There needs to be an easy to use, decentralized, and secure system created.

Hypothetical Example:

A decentralized system similar to Usenet, but one that allows voting and censoring BUT ONLY ON THE CLIENT SIDE. The client software could automatically filter out certain content based off of user defined filters (or it's own configurable, pre-defined filters).

"Web Portals" could be setup to allow access to this system via standard web browsers which anyone could setup. For those that wish to, allowing a set of "filter lists" to be subscribed to could be of use as well.

The web is ultimately a centralized system because the purpose of the DNS and the Domain Name System is to map network locations to the mailing address of organizations and institutions. It's not reasonable to ask every individual to register and maintain their own domain name. Additionally, when individuals die or stop maintain domain names, bitrot occurs and people stop linking to them, meaning there is a natural selection process in place which incentivizes linking to large persistent organizations whose URLs are more likely to be stable instead of to small websites owned by individuals.

The solution is most likely content addressable network, where instead of URLs linking to domain names tied to the mailing address of individuals and corporations, one can share a hashing algorithm tag and document hash, or a public key of a document creator, and let people look up the document through a DHT without going through DNS at all.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_addressable_network

The additional difficulty with client-side peer-to-peer is developing secure native applications to handle a variety of use cases. In order to be competitive with traditional web outlets, you would most likely need to develop a cross-platform virtual machine analagous to the web browser, but which comes with an API for querying peer to peer networks and distributed hash tables built in rather than for performing XML HTTP Requests. Ideally, the VM would also be setup to interpret or compile a binary bytecode fromat so a variety of retargetable compilers could support it as a backend and developers wouldn't be limited to using CSS + Javascript as their human-readable front-end development language.

I also think the best way to implement "web portals" would actually be to create a web server plugin for nginx which allows querying the content addressable DHT and peer-to-peer networks using HTTP. Then web application developers could develop portals interfacing with peer-to-peer to networks in the same way that they would develop web applications which query REST HTTP databases such as Amazon S3.

In Australia, in some university science courses, they still use bullshit non-SI units (e.g. Curie instead of becquerel). I've challenged various professors over this and their answer has always been "it's what is commonly used". My guess is that it's the same case in the US - as a teacher, you can try to make a cultural change for the better and have students ill-equipped to handle the current state of affairs, or you can churn out students who can deal with the current situation. My guess is that your government will need to make the first move - perhaps change all distances on road signs to km, produce cars with km/h speedometers, get gas stations to sell fuel by the litre, etc.

As an aside, despite being raised with the metric system and using it on a daily basis in my career, I still use imperial for some things. If someone asks me my height, I'll say 6'1", not 185 cm. Maybe that's just because my parents were raised with imperial measurements and imparted some of this to me early in life - not sure.
